library(nlmixr2lib)

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Krzyzanski_2026_dexamethasone_3cohort"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1007/s10928-026-10048-5> (open access, CC BY 4.0)

Krzyzanski (2026) introduces *cohort population* estimation: the
distribution of a random parameter is replaced by a small number of point
masses ("cohorts") placed at the nodes of a Gauss-Hermite quadrature rule,
with the quadrature weights as the probabilities of belonging to each
cohort. In NONMEM this is a `$MIX` mixture model whose subpopulation
variances are fixed at zero. The paper has two parts. Study I is a
simulation study on a synthetic one-compartment IV drug that compares the
method with FOCE, IMP and SAEM; it has no real drug and is not packaged.
Study II applies the method to dexamethasone in parturient women, and
gives the two models packaged here:

* `Krzyzanski_2026_dexamethasone_1cohort` -- the naive-pooled (1-cohort)
  fit, with no between-subject variability.
  `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Krzyzanski_2026_dexamethasone_1cohort"))$description`
* `Krzyzanski_2026_dexamethasone_3cohort` -- the Gauss-Hermite 3-cohort
  fit.
  `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Krzyzanski_2026_dexamethasone_3cohort"))$description`

# Population

Fourteen near-term pregnant women delivering by caesarean section received
8 mg dexamethasone phosphate (equivalent to 6.67 mg dexamethasone)
intramuscularly at noon on the day before delivery and a second 8 mg dose at
10 am on the day of delivery, 22 h later. One maternal peripheral-venous and
one umbilical-cord venous plasma sample were drawn from each mother-infant
pair at birth, 0.78-4.42 h after the second dose (Krzyzanski 2026, Study II
Data, Table S2 and Appendix 1). The data come from Tsuei et al. (Clin
Pharmacol Ther 1980;28:88-98). The paper does not report age, body weight,
gestational age or race. The same information is available programmatically
via `readModelDb("Krzyzanski_2026_dexamethasone_3cohort")()$population`.

The 28 observations are printed in the paper (Appendix 1, file `DEX.csv`;
Table S2), and are reproduced below under the article's CC BY 4.0 licence.
Time is hours after the first dose, which is 22 h plus the time after the
last dose.

```{r observed}
obs <- data.frame(
  id = 1:14,
  time = c(
    22.78, 22.83, 23.08, 23.85, 24.45, 24.72, 24.72,
    25.00, 25.00, 25.25, 25.60, 25.62, 25.73, 26.42
  ),
  Cm = c(45.0, 117.0, 70.6, 35.3, 41.5, 30.6, 66.6, 31.3, 15.6, 23.7, 29.7, 39.4, 21.6, 13.6),
  Cf = c(9.8, 23.7, 17.8, 14.5, 11.4, 7.6, 23.3, 11.7, 5.5, 8.6, 12.7, 16.9, 9.0, 6.0)
)
obs_long <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(obs, id, time, conc = Cm, matrix = "Maternal (Cc)"),
  dplyr::transmute(obs, id, time, conc = Cf, matrix = "Umbilical cord (Ccord)")
)
knitr::kable(obs, caption = "Observed dexamethasone concentrations (ng/mL), Krzyzanski 2026 Appendix 1.")
```

# Source trace

Per-parameter origins are also recorded as in-file comments next to each
`ini()` entry in the two model files.

| Equation / parameter | 1-cohort | 3-cohort | Source location |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lcl` (CL/F, L/h) | log(34.7) | log(38.8) | Table 3; THETA(1) |
| `lvc` (V/F, L) | log(103) | log(79.6) | Table 3; THETA(2) |
| `lka` (ka, 1/h) | log(2.92) | log(1.63) | Table 3; THETA(3) |
| `ratio_cord_central` (FMR) | 0.329 | 0.329 | Table 3; THETA(4); Eq 25 |
| `omega_cohort_lcl` (between-cohort SD of log CL/F) | -- | 0.30 | Table 3; THETA(5) = OM1 |
| `p_cohort1`, `p_cohort2` (cohort probabilities) | -- | fixed 0.2954089751509 / sqrt(pi), 1.181635900604 / sqrt(pi) | Appendix 1 `$MIX`; Table S1b |
| `etalcl` | -- | fixed 0 | Appendix 1 `$OMEGA 0.0 FIX` |
| `expSd` (maternal) | sqrt(0.145) | sqrt(0.0611) | Table 3, sigma_m^2; Eq 28 |
| `expSd_Ccord` (cord) | sqrt(0.161) | sqrt(0.0695) | Table 3, sigma_f^2; Eq 29 |
| Cohort clearances `exp(lcl + sqrt(2) * xi_i * omega)` | -- | xi = -1.2247, 0, 1.2247 | Eq 26; Table S1a; Appendix 1 `ksi1`-`ksi3` |
| `d/dt(depot)`, `d/dt(central)` | | | Eqs 22-23 |
| `Cc <- central / vc` | | | Eq 24 |
| `Ccord <- ratio_cord_central * Cc` | | | Eq 25 |
| `Cc ~ lnorm(expSd)`, `Ccord ~ lnorm(expSd_Ccord)` | | | Eqs 28-29; Appendix 1 `Y = IPRED + EPS` |

# Model set-up

The dose is entered as 8000 ug of dexamethasone phosphate on `depot`, as the
paper codes it (`DOSE = 8000.0`). Observation rows sit on the `central`
state with a `dvid` column: `dvid = 1` returns the maternal endpoint and
`dvid = 2` the cord endpoint in the `sim` column, and both `Cc` and `Ccord`
are returned on every observation row. For the 3-cohort model the optional
`mixest` column (1 = low, 2 = middle, 3 = high clearance) pins a subject to a
cohort; without it, `mix()` draws the cohort with the fixed probabilities.

```{r setup-models}
mod1 <- rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb("Krzyzanski_2026_dexamethasone_1cohort"))
mod3 <- rxode2::rxode2(readModelDb("Krzyzanski_2026_dexamethasone_3cohort"))
est1 <- setNames(mod1$iniDf$est, mod1$iniDf$name)
est3 <- setNames(mod3$iniDf$est, mod3$iniDf$name)

dose_amt <- 8000 # ug dexamethasone phosphate per injection
dose_times <- c(0, 22)

# One dose pair and observation rows (both endpoints) per subject.
make_events <- function(ids, obs_time, mixest = NA_integer_) {
  obs_time <- rep_len(obs_time, length(ids))
  dose <- expand.grid(id = ids, time = dose_times)
  dose$evid <- 1L
  dose$amt <- dose_amt
  dose$cmt <- "depot"
  dose$dvid <- NA_integer_
  ob <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(ids), function(i) {
    expand.grid(id = ids[i], time = obs_time[[i]], dvid = 1:2)
  }))
  ob$evid <- 0L
  ob$amt <- 0
  ob$cmt <- "central"
  ev <- dplyr::bind_rows(dose, ob[, names(dose)])
  # rxSolve does not return dvid; this copy rides through `keep`.
  ev$endpoint <- ev$dvid
  # Without a mixest column, mix() draws each subject's cohort.
  if (!all(is.na(mixest))) {
    ev$mixest <- rep_len(as.integer(mixest), length(ids))[match(ev$id, ids)]
  }
  dplyr::arrange(ev, id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))
}
solve <- function(mod, ev) {
  out <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev, keep = "endpoint", returnType = "data.frame")
  # A single-subject solve returns no id column.
  if (!"id" %in% names(out)) out$id <- ev$id[1]
  out
}
```

## Cohort clearances

The paper reports the three allowable individual CL/F values as 23.1, 38.8
and 65.2 L/h (Results, Study II).

```{r cohort-cl}
ev_coh <- make_events(1:3, 23, mixest = 1:3)
cl_coh <- solve(mod3, ev_coh) |>
  dplyr::distinct(id, cl)
knitr::kable(
  cl_coh |> dplyr::mutate(cohort = c("low", "middle", "high")) |>
    dplyr::rename("Cohort (mixest)" = id, "CL/F (L/h)" = cl),
  digits = 2
)
stopifnot(max(abs(cl_coh$cl - c(23.1, 38.8, 65.2))) < 0.05)
```

# Replicate Figure 3: typical maternal and cord profiles

Figure 3 of the paper overlays the observed data with the population
predictions of both models. For the 3-cohort model the population
prediction is the middle cohort (`mixest = 2`), whose clearance is the
typical value THETA(1). As in the paper, the figure shows the window after
the second dose on a log axis; the first-dose profile has the same shape,
22 h earlier.

```{r figure-3, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
grid <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.05)
typ1 <- solve(mod1, make_events(1L, list(grid))) |>
  dplyr::filter(endpoint == 1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = "1-cohort")
typ3 <- solve(mod3, make_events(1L, list(grid), mixest = 2L)) |>
  dplyr::filter(endpoint == 1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = "3-cohort")
typ <- dplyr::bind_rows(typ1, typ3)
typ_long <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(typ, time, model, conc = Cc, matrix = "Maternal (Cc)"),
  dplyr::transmute(typ, time, model, conc = Ccord, matrix = "Umbilical cord (Ccord)")
)

typ_long |>
  dplyr::filter(time >= 22.05, time <= 27) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, conc, colour = matrix)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = model)) +
  geom_point(data = obs_long, aes(time, conc, colour = matrix), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Maternal (Cc)" = "black", "Umbilical cord (Ccord)" = "red")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("1-cohort" = "dashed", "3-cohort" = "solid")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(2, 200)) +
  labs(
    x = "Time after first dose (h)", y = "Dexamethasone (ng/mL)",
    colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
    caption = "Replicates Figure 3 of Krzyzanski 2026."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Objective function and cohort assignment

The strongest available check of the transcription is to evaluate the
likelihood of the published data under the packaged models and compare it
with the objective function values in Table 3 (1-cohort -24.6; 3-cohort
-31.7). The OFV is -2 log-likelihood of the log-transformed observations
without the `N log(2 pi)` constant, as NONMEM reports it. For the mixture
model each woman's likelihood is the probability-weighted sum over the
three cohorts. Every structural, cohort and residual parameter enters this
number, so a mis-transcribed value moves it by far more than the rounding
of Table 3.

The same per-subject likelihoods give each woman's most probable cohort,
which is how the paper assigned the individual clearances shown in Figure 5
(2 women in the low, 10 in the middle and 2 in the high clearance cohort).

```{r ofv}
# Predictions at each woman's birth time; `mixest` pins the cohort.
pred_at_obs <- function(mod, mixest = NA_integer_) {
  solve(mod, make_events(obs$id, obs$time, mixest = mixest)) |>
    dplyr::distinct(id, Cc, Ccord) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id)
}
# Likelihood of each woman's maternal + cord pair (log scale, NONMEM form).
subject_lik <- function(pred, est) {
  stats::dnorm(log(obs$Cm), log(pred$Cc), est[["expSd"]]) *
    stats::dnorm(log(obs$Cf), log(pred$Ccord), est[["expSd_Ccord"]])
}
n_obs <- 2 * nrow(obs)

lik1 <- subject_lik(pred_at_obs(mod1), est1)
ofv1 <- -2 * sum(log(lik1)) - n_obs * log(2 * pi)

p3 <- c(est3[["p_cohort1"]], est3[["p_cohort2"]])
p3 <- c(p3, 1 - sum(p3))
lik3 <- sapply(1:3, function(k) subject_lik(pred_at_obs(mod3, k), est3))
ofv3 <- -2 * sum(log(lik3 %*% p3)) - n_obs * log(2 * pi)
best <- apply(sweep(lik3, 2, p3, `*`), 1, which.max)

ofv_tab <- data.frame(
  Model = c("1-cohort", "3-cohort"),
  `OFV (packaged model)` = round(c(ofv1, ofv3), 2),
  `OFV (Table 3)` = c(-24.6, -31.7),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(ofv_tab)
table(cohort = factor(best, 1:3, c("low", "middle", "high")))

stopifnot(
  abs(ofv1 - (-24.6)) < 0.15,
  abs(ofv3 - (-31.7)) < 0.15,
  identical(as.integer(table(factor(best, 1:3))), c(2L, 10L, 2L))
)
```

Both objective function values reproduce Table 3 to its printed precision,
and the most-probable-cohort assignment reproduces Figure 5 exactly.

```{r figure-5, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3.5}
data.frame(cl = cl_coh$cl[best]) |>
  dplyr::count(cl) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(round(cl, 1)), n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey60", colour = "black") +
  labs(
    x = "Individual CL/F (L/h)", y = "Number of women",
    caption = "Replicates Figure 5 of Krzyzanski 2026."
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Visual predictive check

Figure 4 of the paper shows the observed medians against the 95% confidence
interval of the simulated median from 1000 replicate data sets. With one
sample per woman the observed percentiles cannot be computed, so here each
model is instead simulated for 200 virtual women with residual error, and
the 95% prediction interval of individual concentrations over the sampling
window is overlaid on the observations. For the 3-cohort model each virtual
woman's cohort is drawn by `mix()` with probabilities 1/6, 2/3, 1/6.

```{r vpc}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20261121)
n_vpc <- 200
vpc_grid <- seq(22.5, 26.75, by = 0.25)
ev_vpc <- make_events(seq_len(n_vpc), list(vpc_grid))
sim_vpc <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  solve(mod1, ev_vpc) |>
    dplyr::mutate(model = "1-cohort"),
  solve(mod3, ev_vpc) |>
    dplyr::mutate(model = "3-cohort")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(matrix = ifelse(endpoint == 1, "Maternal (Cc)", "Umbilical cord (Ccord)"))

# Cohort frequencies realised by mix() in the 3-cohort simulation.
sim_vpc |>
  dplyr::filter(model == "3-cohort") |>
  dplyr::distinct(id, cl) |>
  dplyr::count(cl = round(cl, 1)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(fraction = n / n_vpc)

vpc_q <- sim_vpc |>
  dplyr::group_by(model, matrix, time) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    lo = stats::quantile(sim, 0.025),
    med = stats::median(sim),
    hi = stats::quantile(sim, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r figure-4, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
obs_both <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(obs_long, model = "1-cohort"),
  dplyr::mutate(obs_long, model = "3-cohort")
)
ggplot(vpc_q, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = med), colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(data = obs_both, aes(time, conc)) +
  facet_grid(matrix ~ model, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Time after first dose (h)", y = "Dexamethasone (ng/mL)",
    caption = paste(
      "Shaded: 95% prediction interval of 200 simulated women; line: median.",
      "Compare Figure 4 of Krzyzanski 2026."
    )
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r vpc-coverage}
# Fraction of the observations inside the simulated 95% prediction interval,
# with the band interpolated to each woman's sampling time. A well-specified
# model covers about 95%; a mis-transcribed clearance, volume, dose or ratio
# shifts the band by tens of percent and drops coverage far below the bound.
coverage <- obs_both |>
  dplyr::group_by(model, matrix) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(function(d, key) {
    q <- dplyr::filter(vpc_q, model == key$model, matrix == key$matrix)
    lo <- stats::approx(q$time, q$lo, d$time)$y
    hi <- stats::approx(q$time, q$hi, d$time)$y
    data.frame(inside = mean(d$conc >= lo & d$conc <= hi))
  }) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
knitr::kable(coverage, digits = 2)
stopifnot(all(coverage$inside >= 0.75))
```

# PKNCA validation

The paper reports no NCA parameters, so the NCA check is against the closed
form of the one-compartment first-order-absorption model for a single 8000 ug
dose: AUC0-inf = Dose / (CL/F), terminal half-life = log(2) V / CL (ka > CL/V
for every cohort), and tmax = log(ka / kel) / (ka - kel). The groups are the
1-cohort model and the three cohorts of the 3-cohort model.

```{r pknca}
nca_grid <- seq(0, 24, by = 0.05)
groups <- data.frame(
  id = 1:4,
  treatment = c("1-cohort", "3-cohort low", "3-cohort middle", "3-cohort high"),
  mixest = c(NA, 1L, 2L, 3L)
)
make_single <- function(ids, mixest) {
  d <- make_events(ids, list(nca_grid), mixest = mixest)
  d[!(d$evid == 1L & d$time > 0), ]
}
ev_nca1 <- make_single(1L, NA_integer_)
ev_nca3 <- make_single(2:4, 1:3)
sim_nca <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  solve(mod1, ev_nca1),
  solve(mod3, ev_nca3)
) |>
  dplyr::filter(endpoint == 1, !is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::left_join(groups[, c("id", "treatment")], by = "id") |>
  dplyr::select(id, treatment, time, Cc, cl, vc, ka)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(sim_nca, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
dose_df <- data.frame(id = groups$id, treatment = groups$treatment, time = 0, amt = dose_amt)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(
  start = 0, end = Inf,
  cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, aucinf.obs = TRUE, half.life = TRUE
)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))

# Closed-form reference values from each group's parameters.
closed <- sim_nca |>
  dplyr::distinct(treatment, cl, vc, ka) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    kel = cl / vc,
    tmax = log(ka / kel) / (ka - kel),
    cmax = dose_amt / vc * ka / (ka - kel) * (exp(-kel * tmax) - exp(-ka * tmax)),
    aucinf.obs = dose_amt / cl,
    half.life = log(2) / kel
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(treatment, cmax, tmax, aucinf.obs, half.life)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca_res,
  reference = closed,
  by = "treatment",
  units = c(cmax = "ng/mL", tmax = "h", aucinf.obs = "ng*h/mL", half.life = "h"),
  tolerance_pct = 5
)
knitr::kable(cmp, caption = "PKNCA on the packaged models vs. the closed form. * differs by >5%.")

nca_wide <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result) |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("aucinf.obs", "half.life")) |>
  dplyr::select(treatment, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::bind_rows(
      dplyr::transmute(closed, treatment, PPTESTCD = "aucinf.obs", ref = aucinf.obs),
      dplyr::transmute(closed, treatment, PPTESTCD = "half.life", ref = half.life)
    ),
    by = c("treatment", "PPTESTCD")
  )
# The solve feeds the identity directly, so only numerical error separates
# the two sides.
stopifnot(all(abs(nca_wide$PPORRES / nca_wide$ref - 1) < 0.03))
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Dose amount.** The paper codes the dose as 8000 ug of dexamethasone
  phosphate (`DOSE = 8000.0`), not the 6.67 mg of dexamethasone it is
  equivalent to (the Discussion lists this among the reasons V/F exceeds the
  plasma volume). CL/F and V/F are therefore apparent values relative to the
  phosphate dose; dose the models with the phosphate amount in ug, or scale
  CL/F and V/F by 6.67 / 8 to dose in dexamethasone base.
* **ODE instead of the closed form.** The paper's closed-form solution
  (Eq 30, and `A2` in the Appendix 1 control stream) adds the first-dose
  concentration at t2 = 22 h as a constant after the second dose instead of
  letting it decay. The packaged models solve the ODEs of Eqs 22-23 by
  superposition, which is the system Eq 30 is meant to solve. The
  difference is the first-dose residual at 22 h: about 0.05 ng/mL for the
  1-cohort model and 0.003 / 0.2 ng/mL for the middle / low 3-cohort
  cohorts, against observations of 5.5-117 ng/mL. The objective function
  values above, computed with the ODE solution, still match Table 3.
* **Mixture encoding.** The 3-cohort model uses rxode2's native `mix()` with
  the fixed Gauss-Hermite weights as mixing probabilities and the
  between-cohort SD `omega_cohort_lcl` as a fixed effect, exactly as in the
  `$MIX` control stream. A zero-variance `etalcl ~ fixed(0)` mirrors the
  stream's `$OMEGA 0.0 FIX` and is kept because `mix()` requires an eta; it
  makes rxode2 print a "simulation without 'omega'" message, which is
  harmless. The maintainers ratified the names `p_cohort1`, `p_cohort2` and
  `omega_cohort_lcl` for this first library use of `mix()`.
* **1-cohort model has no eta.** The paper fixes the 1-cohort IIV at zero, so
  the model carries no random effect; simulations vary only through the
  residual error.
* **Fetal-to-maternal ratio name.** FMR is a natural-scale THETA with no
  random effect, so it is written bare as `ratio_cord_central`, following
  `ratio_isf_peripheral1`.
* **VPC form.** The paper's Figure 4 shows the confidence interval of the
  simulated median from 1000 replicate data sets; the check above uses a
  95% prediction interval from 200 virtual women per model, which carries
  the same information about calibration within the per-arm cohort limit
  used for these articles.
* **Study I not packaged.** Study I is a simulation study on a synthetic drug
  with arbitrary parameter values; it has no real-drug model.
* **Errata.** No correction notice is linked to the article's PubMed record
  (PMID 42406183) as of 2026-11-21.
